segments.say: Think back, for a moment, to the house you grew up in. How did people there get angry? Maybe voices were raised, and then it was over in five minutes. Maybe nobody ever raised their voice at all, and anger showed up as silence, or a closed door. Maybe there was a rule that you never let an insult pass. Most of us learned a whole language of anger long before we could name it. What's allowed, what's rude, what's weak, what's brave. Nobody sat us down and explained it. We simply watched, and listened, and absorbed it.

Sam learned his in a house where teasing was normal, but being made to look foolish was not. His brother knew that too. That's partly why You forgot again? stings the way it does. It isn't just three words. It touches an old rule, written somewhere deep down, about what counts as being disrespected. And rules like that don't only come from families. Sometimes they come from whole regions.

In 1996, the psychologists Dov Cohen, Richard Nisbett, Brian Bowdle and Norbert Schwarz published a study in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. Its title called it an experimental ethnography. They were interested in an idea known as a culture of honor, where a person's reputation, and their readiness to defend it, matters a great deal.

Researchers had suggested that in parts of the southern United States, there was historically a stronger culture of honor than in the north. In a culture like that, letting an insult pass might mean losing face. So the question was simple. If you insult two young men, one from the South and one from the North, will they react differently?

The setup was almost theatrical. Male students at the University of Michigan were asked to walk down a hallway as part of an experiment. On the way, a man bumped into them with his shoulder, and muttered an insult. The man was working for the researchers. The students didn't know that.

It was over in a second. A bump and a word. The kind of thing that happens on busy streets every day. But the researchers watched carefully what happened next. They watched how the students reacted. And they measured two hormones, before and after the bump.

One was cortisol, which tends to rise with stress. The other was testosterone, which is often linked with readiness for competition and confrontation. If the insult landed differently for different people, those hormones might show it, even if the students stayed polite on the outside.

show.title: What they measured
items: Signs of anger in the face
Testosterone, linked to readiness to compete

segments.say: And they did. The students from the South showed more signs of anger after being insulted. Their cortisol and their testosterone rose more than those of the students from the North. Same hallway. Same bump. Same muttered word. But for some students, the insult landed much harder, because of what an insult had come to mean where they grew up. On the outside, many of them probably looked fairly calm. They walked on. They carried on with the experiment. But underneath, their bodies were telling a different story, a story of being challenged and getting ready to respond.

show.title: Cohen and colleagues, 1996
show.label: in cortisol and testosterone after the insult, in students from the South

segments.say: I want to be careful here. This isn't a study about which region is better or worse. It's a study about meaning. The same small event can mean nothing much to one person, and a serious challenge to another. And that meaning isn't chosen in the moment. It's something we carry with us, quietly, from the places that shaped us.

A quiet corridor. A bump on the shoulder. A muttered word. It's such an ordinary place, and such an ordinary moment. And yet it turned into a little window onto something big. Our anger doesn't only depend on what happens to us. It depends on what we've learned that it means.

Culture also shapes something else. Not just how quickly we get angry, but what we do with it. Do we say it out loud, or keep it in? And here a lot of us have a fixed belief. Some people are sure that bottling up anger is bad for you. Others are sure that showing anger is bad for you. Both beliefs are said with great certainty, often by the same well-meaning friends, sometimes in the same week. Let it out, it's not healthy to keep it in. Or, calm down, getting worked up isn't good for you. A fascinating study suggests the answer might depend on where you live.

In 2015, the psychologist Shinobu Kitayama and a large team published a study in Psychological Science. They used two big surveys of adults, one in the United States and one in Japan. People answered questions about how often they expressed their anger outwardly. And they had health checks, which included biological markers measured in the lab.

show.where: Large surveys in the US and Japan

segments.say: From those checks, the researchers built a measure of what they called biological health risk. It combined signs of inflammation in the body with markers linked to the heart and blood vessels. Then they asked whether people who expressed more anger had more risk, or less.

show.title: What they looked at
items: Signs of heart and blood vessel risk

segments.say: In the United States, people who expressed more anger tended to have higher biological health risk. In Japan, it was the other way round. People who expressed more anger tended to have lower biological health risk. And these patterns weren't explained by age, gender, smoking, drinking, chronic illness or social status.

That's a striking result. The same habit, expressing anger outwardly, went along with more risk in one country and less risk in the other. It's an association, not proof of cause. But it does suggest that anger doesn't have one fixed meaning, or one fixed effect, everywhere in the world.

show.text: The same habit pointed in opposite directions in two countries.

segments.say: So if you've ever been told, with great confidence, that you must always let your anger out, or that you must always keep it in, this study is a gentle reminder to hold those rules a little more loosely. What anger does to us seems to depend, at least partly, on the world around us, and on what anger means in that world. There may be no single rule that fits every person, in every place.

So when Sam's thumb hovers over send, he's not only reacting as a hungry, tired man on a warm bus. He's reacting with a rulebook he inherited. About teasing, and respect, and what it means to be called forgetful by your little brother. That rulebook isn't wrong. But it isn't the only possible reading either.

So perhaps there's a fourth question to add. Not just, when did I eat, how did I sleep, and what's around me. But also, which of my old rules just got touched? Sometimes simply naming the rule, oh, this is about feeling foolish, is enough to loosen its grip a little.

show.title: Questions so far
items: Which old rule just got touched?

segments.say: But naming things is for a little later tonight. First, there's a very popular piece of advice about anger that we need to look at honestly. You've almost certainly heard it. It sounds sensible, and it feels true. It's the idea that when you're angry, the best thing to do is to let it all out.

show.sub: What do we do with it?
